candidate_relations.reason: The thin-walled unilocular ovarian lesion and normal major tumor markers favor benignity, but a benign ovarian cyst does not identify the epithelial-stromal cystadenofibroma subtype.
A smooth 1.5-mm wall with no septa or solid component and normal CA-125 does not support cystadenocarcinoma, and malignant behavior conflicts with the reference.
Imaging suggests an ovarian-origin unilocular fluid-filled lesion without a solid soft-tissue component expected for pelvic sarcoma.
Progressive abdominal distension is caused by the 21-cm ovarian mass, but this descriptive syndrome does not state its cystadenofibroma histology.
Two years of painless gradual distension without acute pelvic pain or twisted pedicle findings is incompatible with ovarian torsion.
The mass is entirely unilocular fluid without solid components and AFP is normal, arguing against an immature teratoma.
Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL with an MCV of 73.2 fL indicates microcytic anemia, but iron studies are absent and anemia does not identify the ovarian tumor.
Dysgerminoma is usually a solid vascular mass, whereas CT shows a thin-walled fluid lesion with no solid component and no corroborating germ-cell marker pattern.
Ultrasound and CT support ovarian origin, but the term ovarian tumor does not specify cystadenofibroma.
A very large unilocular cyst can resemble mucinous cystadenoma, but the candidate specifies a different epithelial subtype and omits the fibrous stromal component of cystadenofibroma.
Serous cystadenoma is a plausible benign cystic differential, but it is not the epithelial-stromal cystadenofibroma specified by the reference.
The lesion is radiologically an ovarian cyst, but morphology alone cannot supply the cystadenofibroma histology.
